title: Anthropic ships Claude Opus 5.5 at Fable 5.1 quality for 40% less than Opus 5
subtitle: The new flagship arrived within hours of OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and Luna, turning September's model race into an open price war.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22 as the first entry in a new 5.5 family, positioning it as Fable 5.1-class capability at a materially lower cost than the July Opus 5 release. Anthropic pegged input and output token pricing at $4 and $20 per million respectively — a 20% cut from Opus 5 — with cache reads dropping 60% to $0.20 per million. The company also claimed output speeds are more than 30% higher, and confirmed availability on AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Azure at launch.

The efficiency framing matters because it changes the calculus for teams already running Opus in production. A 40% workload cost reduction with Fable-level quality means Anthropic is asking developers to stop reaching for its most expensive tier for hard tasks — the mid-tier is now good enough. Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 are expected in the coming weeks, which will complete the family and force another round of price comparisons across the stack.

The release also landed within hours of OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and Luna launches on the same day, both priced at roughly half the prior GPT-5.6 tier. Fortune framed the twin drops as evidence that the coordinated 'AI slowdown' rhetoric of the past few weeks does not extend to product roadmaps or margins. Underneath the pricing story is a bigger one: the frontier labs now believe capability parity is close enough that they compete on cost per token, not just benchmark headlines.

For learners, this is the shape the market takes when a category matures. Watch what happens to your bill, not what happens to the leaderboard — the labs will tell you a model is 'smarter,' but the honest signal of whether they mean it is whether they cut the price. Rebuild your evals against the cheaper tier before you re-run them on the flagship; most of the time, the answer to 'do I need Opus?' is now 'no.'
